question: 该不该把家底留给孩子？
question_en: Should you leave your estate to your children?
sub: 制度上人人反对世袭，回到自家餐桌，却几乎人人想留。
sub_en: In principle almost everyone opposes inherited privilege; at their own dinner table almost everyone wants to leave the house to their children.

casting.reason: 他不问该不该，只问钱实际怎么流。在他的账本里，父母对孩子的转移横跨一生：早年的教育投入、中年的赠与、身后的遗赠，三段的回报率依次递减。他因此对『遗产』这个词本身有保留——很大一部分遗产其实是意外的，来自人不知道自己能活多久、只好一直攥着防身的那笔钱。他也不肯放过一个更不体面的动机：把财产悬在头顶换取子女的探望。他的解法始终指向同一个方向：把钱往前挪，改成一次性的、指定用途的，别做成终身发放的现金流。
casting.reason_en: He does not ask what ought to be done; he asks how the money actually moves. In his ledger a parent's transfers to a child run across a lifetime — schooling early, gifts in middle age, a bequest at the end — and the return falls at every stage. Hence his reservation about the word inheritance itself: much of what gets left is accidental, the residue of money held back because nobody knows how long he will live. Nor will he pass over a less dignified motive, wealth held above the head in exchange for visits. His remedy always points the same way: move the money forward, make it one-off and tied to a purpose, and never turn it into a stream paid for life.

casting.reason: 禁止父母把资源交给自己的孩子，资源并不会消失，只会转到一个不认识这个孩子的机构手里——他一开口就把重心从『继承是否制造不平等』挪到『替代方案由谁决定』。他承认继承确实带来不平等，也提醒一件常被忽略的事：在各种被继承的东西里，物质财产恰恰最容易被挥霍、最容易转手，而教养、口音与门路才真正牢固，且无法充公。他守的是父母判断的自由，不是富人的地位；被追问到底时，他宁愿降低进入的门槛，也不愿削平顶端。
casting.reason_en: Forbid parents to hand resources to their own children and the resources do not vanish; they pass to an institution that has never met the child — with that, he moves the centre of the argument from whether inheritance produces inequality to who decides under the alternative. He concedes the inequality, and points out something usually missed: of everything that gets inherited, material property is the most easily squandered and the most easily transferred, while manners, accent and introductions are what hold, and those cannot be confiscated. What he defends is the parent's freedom to judge, not the standing of the rich; pressed to the end, he would rather lower the barriers to entry than level the top.

casting.reason: 遗产里最小、最显眼、也最好征税的一块才是钱——他一开口就把争论挪到别处。真正的交割发生在孩子上学之前：腔调、坐姿、面对老师与医生时那种不慌的熟悉感，这些东西伪装成天赋，因此免税；学历更妙，它给继承来的优势盖上考试的章。他最不留情的一击针对温和派：说『我不打算给孩子留钱』的人，多半只是没意识到最贵的一笔早已交割完毕。他愿意承认的唯一诚实，是别把继承来的优势讲成自力更生的故事。
casting.reason_en: Money is the smallest, most visible and most taxable part of any inheritance — and with that he moves the argument elsewhere. The real handover happens before the child starts school: intonation, bearing, the unhurried ease in front of a teacher or a doctor. These pass themselves off as talent and so go untaxed; the diploma is neater still, stamping an inherited advantage with the seal of an examination. His least forgiving blow lands on the moderates: anyone who says he does not intend to leave his children money has usually failed to notice that the most expensive transfer already went through. The one honesty he will settle for is that an inherited advantage should not be narrated as a story of self-reliance.

casting.reason: 他不是在假设，他试过。土地交出去、一八八一年以后的版权放弃掉，为此与妻子争了二十多年，八十二岁那年冬夜离家，死在一个小车站上。结论并没有因此软化：用别人的劳动堆起来的舒适会让人失掉自己站着的能力，你替孩子挡下的每一件事，都取消了他本该学会的一样东西。被指出样本只有一个时，他答那一个样本是自己的一生。到最后他愿意承认失败的部分，只留下一件不花钱的事：让孩子看见你劳动。
casting.reason_en: He is not speculating; he tried it. He signed the land over to his household, renounced the copyright on everything written after 1881, quarrelled with his wife about it for more than twenty years, and at eighty-two walked out on a winter night and died at a small railway halt. The conclusion never softened: comfort built out of other people's labour costs a person the ability to stand on his own, and every difficulty you head off for a child cancels something he was meant to learn. Told that his sample is a single case, he answers that the case is his own life. At the end he will concede the part he lost, and leaves behind one thing that costs nothing: let your children see you work.

casting.reason: 在他看来财产从来不是一个人的私物，而是祖宗所积、当以养一族的东西，因此他反对的不是留，而是把家产原样交成某一房的私产。他搬出的样板是范仲淹的义庄：田不入私门，岁入养族中孤寡、供子弟读书，掌事者一年一换、账目可查，一家数百年不坠。他也提醒中国旧法本是诸子均分，均分则势不聚。他给出的判准落在同一处：善遗者不遗其产，遗其法度——先问这笔钱谁掌、谁能动、几年一议。
casting.reason_en: Property, to him, was never one man's private thing but what the ancestors accumulated in order to keep a whole lineage; so what he objects to is not leaving anything but handing the estate over intact as the private holding of one branch. His model is Fan Zhongyan's charitable estate: land that enters no private hands, a yearly yield that keeps the lineage's widows and orphans and pays for its sons' schooling, a steward replaced every year and a ledger open to inspection — a house that did not fall for centuries. He also notes that the old Chinese law divided among all sons rather than the eldest, so that no concentration could form. His test always lands in the same place: the man who leaves well leaves not his property but his rules — ask first who holds the money, who may draw on it, and how often it is argued again.

casting.reason: 父母高估自己对孩子成年结局的影响，这是她从发展研究里带来的一盆冷水，而且两边都要泼：怕钱毁掉孩子，与相信留够钱就能保他一生，是同一种把孩子当图纸产品的幻觉。她坚持的那条证据很硬——贫困对幼儿发育的伤害是真的，而在温饱之上，额外的财富几乎改变不了什么。于是她把整场辩论换成一个更锋利的问题：你要给的是让人不必努力的天花板，还是让人敢于失败的地板？
casting.reason_en: Parents overestimate their causal grip on how a child turns out — that is the cold water she brings from developmental research, and she throws it in both directions: fearing that money will ruin a child and believing that enough money will secure one are two faces of the same illusion, the child as an object built to a blueprint. The evidence she holds to is hard: poverty genuinely damages how a young brain develops, while above a decent floor extra wealth changes almost nothing. So she reframes the whole argument into a sharper question — are you handing over a ceiling that makes effort optional, or a floor that makes failure survivable?

casting.reason: 她一上来就换掉了这场辩论的账本：干到六十五、七十五告别、剩下的留给孩子——这套剧本是短寿命时代的产物。今天六十岁的一对夫妻，至少一人活过九十的概率相当可观，而遗产真正的对手不是遗产税，是失能之后那几年的照护账单。她还带来一条长期追踪里很稳的发现：人感到剩余时间收窄时，要的不是把东西留下，是现在被看见。所以她主张把一部分转移提前到孩子最需要的那几年，趁自己还听得见回音。
casting.reason_en: She begins by replacing the ledger the argument is using: work to sixty-five, take your leave at seventy-five, pass on the rest — a script written for shorter lives. For a couple who are sixty today the odds that at least one of them sees ninety are substantial, and the real competitor for an estate is not the estate tax but the bill for care in the years after independence goes. She brings one more finding that holds up across long panels: as people feel their remaining time narrow, what they want is not to leave things behind but to be seen now. Hence her case for moving part of the transfer forward into the years a child actually needs it, while you can still hear the answer.

casting.reason: 他先不问该留多少，而问『家底』究竟是什么：田宅金帛并非你所有，只是你执之为我的，这份执与父母执『我的孩子』本是同一件事。他真正关心的是另一条传承线——你日夜的贪与惧熏习成种，孩子在旁朝夕见闻，同样的种子也就熏了进去；田宅可夺，熏习夺不走。他并不劝人散尽家财，财物用于布施即成资粮，执为我所才成系缚。他留下的问题只有一句：你要留的，是替他解绳，还是替自己续执？
casting.reason_en: He declines to start with how much and asks instead what the family estate is: fields, houses, gold and cloth are not yours, you merely grip them as mine — and that grip is of a piece with a parent's grip on 'my child'. What he is really after is a second line of descent: your greed and your fear, day and night, lay down seeds, and the child beside you, watching and listening, has the same seeds perfumed into him. Fields can be taken; that cannot. He does not counsel giving everything away — wealth spent in giving becomes provision for the road, wealth gripped as mine becomes a rope. He leaves a single question: does what you leave loosen his rope, or continue your own grip?

casting.reason: 他把自己的运气叫作卵巢彩票：一九三零年生在美国，性别与肤色恰好抽对，同一副脑子换个时空多半一文不值。由此而来的是那条被反复引用的线——给孩子足够多的钱去做任何事，但别多到让他们可以什么都不做。他捐出九十九，也公开支持对自己家征遗产税，理由不是孩子不配，而是世袭财富把机会派给了出生顺位的赢家。被指出捐不掉姓氏与通讯录时，他不争辩，只说钱是这堆东西里唯一能被具体数字管住的一项。
casting.reason_en: He calls his own luck the ovarian lottery: born in the United States in 1930, with the sex and the skin colour that happened to come up, the same wiring in another time or place worth close to nothing. From that follows the line everyone quotes — enough money to do anything, not so much that they can do nothing. He is giving away ninety-nine percent and has argued in public for an estate tax that lands on his own family, not because his children are undeserving but because dynastic wealth hands the best chances to whoever won the draw at birth. Told that he cannot give away the surname or the address book, he does not argue; he says money is the one item on the pile that can be bound with an actual number.

posts.text: 先把位置摆正：继承确实制造不平等，这我不否认。可要紧的是替代方案——禁止父母把资源交给自己的子女，资源并不会消失，只是转到某个不认识你孩子的委员会手里。父母对自己孩子的了解，是任何分配机构都拿不到的，这正是我一生反复讲的知识问题。**况且在各种继承里，物质财产恰恰是最容易被挥霍掉的那一种；继承来的教养、口音与门路才真正牢固，而它们无法充公。**
posts.text_en: Let me place the question properly first. Inheritance does produce inequality; I do not deny it. What matters is the alternative — forbid parents to hand resources to their own children and the resources do not vanish, they pass to some committee that has never met your child. What a parent knows about his own child is not available to any distributing authority, and that is the knowledge problem I have spent my life on. **Besides, of everything that gets inherited, material property is the one most easily squandered; the manners, the accent and the introductions are what hold, and those cannot be confiscated.**

glossary.知识问题: the knowledge problem（知识问题）：社会运转所需的知识从来不是集中的，而是零散分布在千万人手里——谁最清楚自己的处境、时机与人事。中央计划的困难不在于计划者不够聪明，而在于这些知识大多说不出口、也无法逐层上报。价格之所以重要，正因为它把这些分散的知识压成一个人人可读的信号。

glossary_en.the knowledge problem: The knowledge a society runs on is never concentrated; it is scattered across millions of people, each knowing something particular about his own circumstances, timing and relationships. The difficulty with central planning is not that planners are stupid but that most of this knowledge cannot be articulated, let alone reported upward. Prices matter because they compress that dispersed knowledge into a signal anyone can read.

posts.text: 我走过另一条路，代价是我的家。我把土地交给家人，放弃了一八八一年以后所有作品的版权，为此与妻子争了二十多年，八十二岁那年冬夜离家，死在一个小车站的站长室里。结论我没有改。**用别人的劳动堆起来的舒适，会把人变成不能自己站着的东西。**哈耶克先生说父母最了解自己的孩子，我不否认；我否认的是这份了解一定会被用在让孩子变强上。多数时候它被用来替孩子挡住每一件本该由他自己扛的事。
posts.text_en: I took the other road, and it cost me my family. I made the land over to my household, renounced the copyright on everything I wrote after 1881, quarrelled with my wife about it for more than twenty years, and at eighty-two left home on a winter night and died in a stationmaster's room at a small railway halt. My conclusion has not changed. **Comfort built out of other people's labour turns a person into something that cannot stand on its own.** Hayek says a parent knows his child best, and I do not dispute it. I dispute that the knowledge is bound to be used to make the child stronger. Far more often it is used to hold off every single thing the child ought to have carried himself.

posts.text: 我不谈应该，我谈钱实际怎么流。父母对孩子的转移一生分三段：早年的人力资本投资、中年的赠与、身后的遗赠。回报率最高的是第一段，最低的是最后一段——钱在六十岁到手，能改变的事已经不多。而且很大一块遗产根本不是安排出来的，是意外遗赠：人不知道自己哪年死，只好一直把钱攥着防身，没花完的就成了遗产。**你以为你在表达爱，多半只是在为一个你猜不准的寿命做准备。**还有一种更不体面的动机，叫战略性遗赠：钱悬在头顶，换子女常回来看看。
posts.text_en: I will not talk about what ought to be; I will talk about how the money actually moves. Transfers from parent to child fall into three stages across a lifetime: investment in human capital early on, gifts in middle age, and a bequest at the end. The first has the highest return and the last the lowest — money that lands when you are sixty cannot change very much. And a large share of what gets left is not planned at all. It is an accidental bequest: nobody knows which year he will die, so he holds the money back as insurance, and whatever is unspent becomes an estate. **You believe you are expressing love; mostly you are hedging against a lifespan you cannot predict.** There is a less dignified motive too, the strategic bequest motive: money held above the head in exchange for visits.

glossary.意外遗赠: accidental bequest（意外遗赠）：因为不知道自己能活多久、也不知道晚年要花掉多少医疗与照护费，人会一直保留一笔谁也不敢动的钱；等他去世，这笔没用掉的储备就变成了遗产。它不是一份计划中的礼物，而是预防性储蓄的残值——这解释了为什么许多遗产的金额与父母真正想给的数目相差甚远。
glossary.战略性遗赠: strategic bequest motive（战略性遗赠）：父母把遗产当作可以随时改写的悬赏，用来换取子女的探望、照料与顺从。经济学家用它解释一个反常的发现：有多个子女的老人往往得到更多探望，因为子女之间在争夺同一笔可分配的财产。

glossary_en.accidental bequest: Because nobody knows how long he will live or what the last years of care will cost, people hold back a reserve they dare not touch; when they die the unspent reserve becomes an estate. It is not a planned gift but the residue of precautionary saving — which explains why the size of many estates bears little relation to what the parents actually intended to give.
glossary_en.strategic bequest motive: Parents treat the will as a standing bounty they can rewrite at any moment, exchanged for visits, care and compliance. Economists invoke it to explain an odd finding: elderly parents with several children tend to receive more visits, because the children are competing over the same divisible estate.

posts.text: 你们要争的那笔钱，是遗产里最小、最显眼、也最容易被征税的一块。真正的交割在孩子上小学以前就完成了：说话的腔调、坐姿、面对老师和医生时那种不慌不忙的熟悉感。这些叫文化资本，它伪装成天赋与努力，因此免税。学历更妙——它把继承来的东西盖上一个考试的章，谁都不好意思再说那是给的。**所以『我不打算给孩子留钱』这句话，多半只是没意识到最贵的那一笔早就交割完了。**
posts.text_en: The money you propose to argue about is the smallest, the most visible and by far the most taxable part of an inheritance. The real handover is complete before the child starts school: the intonation, the way of sitting, the unhurried familiarity in front of a teacher or a doctor. This is cultural capital, and because it passes itself off as talent and effort it goes untaxed. The diploma is the neatest trick of all — it stamps what was inherited with the seal of an examination, after which nobody is embarrassed to call it earned. **So 'I don't intend to leave my children money' usually just means the most expensive transfer went through unnoticed.**

glossary.文化资本: cultural capital（文化资本）：一个人从家庭里带出来、可以在学校与职场兑换成优势的非货币资源——语言习惯、审美偏好、举止分寸、对各种制度的熟悉。它有三种形态：内化在身体里的（口音、姿态）、物化在器物里的（书、乐器）、制度化为凭证的（学历）。它的力量来自不被看见：一旦被读成天赋，它带来的优势就免于解释。

glossary_en.cultural capital: The non-monetary resources a person carries out of the family and cashes in at school and at work — habits of speech, taste, bearing, an easy familiarity with institutions. It exists in three states: embodied in the person (accent, posture), objectified in things (books, instruments) and institutionalised as credentials (the diploma). Its power lies in going unseen: once it is read as talent, the advantage it confers never has to be explained.

posts.text: 我先给这场辩论换一本账。你们默认的剧本是：干到六十五岁退休、七十五岁告别，剩下的留给孩子。这本账过期很久了。今天一对六十岁的夫妻，其中至少一人活过九十的概率相当可观；而遗产真正的对手不是遗产税，是失能之后那几年的照护账单。**先算你自己还要活多久，再谈留多少——次序反了，最后留下的往往是一笔负债和一场家庭争吵。**另有一件在长期追踪里很稳的事：当人感到时间视野收窄，他要的不是把东西留下，是现在被看见。
posts.text_en: Let me change the ledger this debate is using. Your default script is: work until sixty-five, retire, take your leave at seventy-five, and pass on what is left. That script expired a long time ago. For a couple who are sixty today, the odds that at least one of them lives past ninety are substantial — and the real competitor for an estate is not estate tax, it is the bill for care in the years after independence goes. **Work out how long you still have to live before you decide how much to leave; reverse the order and what you pass on tends to be a debt and a family quarrel.** One more finding that holds up across long panels: when people feel their time horizon narrowing, what they want is not to leave things behind but to be seen now.

glossary.时间视野: time horizon（时间视野）：一个人主观感到自己还剩多少时间。视野开阔时，人偏好探索、结识新人、为将来投资；视野收窄时——年老、重病、临别在即——人转而收缩到最重要的几段关系与当下的情感意义。它随处境而变，不只随年龄：把年轻人放进一个即将离别的处境，他的偏好很快就像老人。

glossary_en.time horizon: How much time a person subjectively feels he has left. When the horizon is open, people prefer exploration, new acquaintances and investment in a future payoff; when it narrows — through age, illness, an imminent parting — they contract onto a few central relationships and the emotional meaning of the present. It shifts with circumstance and not only with age: put a young person in a situation of imminent departure and his preferences soon look old.

posts.text: 我要往两边各泼一盆冷水。托尔斯泰伯爵怕钱毁掉孩子，另一半人相信留够钱就能保他一生——这是同一种幻觉的两面。我把两种养育叫作园丁与木匠：木匠照图纸把孩子做成预定的成品，园丁只负责把土壤弄得肥沃、安全、够杂。发展研究里最扎实的一条是：**贫困对幼儿发育的伤害是真的，而在温饱线以上，额外的财富几乎改变不了什么。**给最底层的母亲每月几百块现金，婴儿的脑电活动都会不同；给顶层再加一栋房，改变的只是税务筹划。
posts.text_en: Let me throw cold water on both sides. Count Tolstoy is afraid money will ruin a child; half the room believes enough money will secure one for life. These are two faces of the same illusion. I call the two styles of parenting the gardener and the carpenter: the carpenter works to a blueprint and turns out a specified object, while the gardener only makes the soil rich, safe and varied. The sturdiest finding in developmental research is this: **poverty genuinely damages how a young brain develops, and above the level of basic security extra wealth changes almost nothing.** A few hundred dollars a month to the poorest mothers shifts the electrical activity of their infants' brains; another house at the top changes the tax planning and little else.

glossary.园丁与木匠: the gardener and the carpenter（园丁与木匠）：两种养育的隐喻。木匠有一张图纸，把材料加工成事先定好的成品，做得好不好按成品是否合规格来评判；园丁不知道种子会长成什么，只负责土壤、水与光照，让一片园子生态多样、扛得住意外。孩子的学习机制更接近后者：漫长的童年之所以存在，正是为了在受保护的环境里大量试错。

glossary_en.the gardener and the carpenter: Two metaphors for raising children. A carpenter works from a blueprint, shapes material into a specified product and is judged by whether the product meets spec. A gardener does not know what the seed will become and tends the soil, the water and the light so that a varied garden survives whatever comes. Children's learning works far more like the second: the long human childhood exists precisely so that a great deal of trial and error can happen under protection.

posts.text: 财者，非一人之私也。祖宗所积，本以养一族，不以富一房。汉人有言：遗子黄金满籯，不如一经。范文正公立义庄，置田千亩，族中孤寡有所养，子弟有塾可读，掌者岁易而籍可稽，其家数世不坠。**是故善遗者，不遗其产，遗其法度。**又吾国之法，诸子均分，不专于长；均分则势不聚，此古人之深意。今人析产而不立规，故一传而尽。教之以业，束之以礼，虽无余财，其家不贫。
posts.text_en: Property is not one man's private thing. What the ancestors accumulated was meant to keep a whole lineage, not to enrich one branch of it. The Han had a saying: a chest of gold left to your son is worth less than one classic. Fan Zhongyan founded a charitable estate, bought a thousand mu of land, and with it the widows and orphans of the lineage were kept and its sons had a school to attend; the steward was replaced annually and the accounts could be inspected. His house did not fall for generations. **So the man who leaves well leaves not his property but his rules.** Our old law, moreover, was partible inheritance among all sons rather than the eldest alone; divide equally and no concentration forms — the ancients meant that. Today men divide the property and lay down no rule, so it is gone in a single generation. Teach him a trade, bind him with ritual, and though there be no money to spare the household will not be poor.
posts.vernacular: 财产不是一个人的私物。祖上攒下来的东西，本意是养活整个宗族，不是让某一房富起来。汉朝人说过：留给儿子满箱黄金，不如留一部经书。范仲淹办义庄，买下上千亩田，族里的孤儿寡妇有人养，子弟有私塾可以读书，管事的每年轮换、账目随时可查，他家几代都没有败落。**所以真会留东西的人，留的不是财产，是规矩。**再说我们的旧法是诸子均分，不专给长子；一均分，势力就聚不起来，这是古人的深意。今天的人只分家产、不立规矩，所以一代就散光了。教他一门手艺，用礼约束他，就算没有多余的钱，这个家也穷不了。

glossary.义庄: charitable estate（义庄）：宋代以后宗族共有的一份不可分割的田产，收入用于赡养族中孤寡、资助子弟读书与婚丧。范仲淹于皇祐年间首创，并定下规条：田不入私门、按丁口发米、掌事者定期轮换、账目公开可查。它的要害不在钱多，而在把一笔财产从个人手里挪进一套可以世代运行的规则里。
glossary.诸子均分: partible inheritance（诸子均分）：中国自秦汉以来通行的继承之法，家产在诸子之间大致均分，长子只在祭祀与主持上有优先，不独占田宅。与欧洲的长子继承制相比，它让大宗财产每一代都被切碎，既抑制了世袭贵族的形成，也使家族难以积累起可长期支配的资本。

glossary_en.charitable estate: From the Song dynasty onward, an indivisible block of land held in common by a lineage, its income used to support the lineage's widows and orphans, to fund a school for its sons and to pay for weddings and funerals. Fan Zhongyan founded the first and wrote its rules: the land never enters private hands, grain is issued by head count, the steward rotates, and the accounts are open to inspection. What made it work was not its size but that it moved property out of an individual's hands into a rule that could run for generations.
glossary_en.partible inheritance: The standard Chinese law of succession from the Qin and Han onward: the family property is divided roughly equally among all sons, the eldest taking precedence only in ritual and headship rather than in land. Compared with European primogeniture it broke up large holdings in every generation, which both checked the formation of a hereditary aristocracy and made it hard for any family to accumulate capital it could command over the long run.

posts.text: 诸君所争之家底，当先问其体性。田宅金帛，非汝所有，特汝所执耳，是名我所执。父执吾之子，子执吾之产，二执相续，苦亦相续。且真所遗者，不在券契之上。汝日夜之贪与惧，熏习成种，藏于阿赖耶识；子在侧，朝夕见闻，其种亦随之而熏。**田宅可夺，熏习不可夺；汝所真遗者，是此。**然吾不劝弃财。财用于施，则成资粮；执之为我所，则成系缚。故当自问：所留者，为解其缚，抑为续汝之执？
posts.text_en: Before you dispute the family estate, ask what it is. Fields, houses, gold and cloth are not yours; you merely grip them, and that grip is called mamakāra, mine-making. The father grips 'my son', the son grips 'my property', and as the two grips continue so does the suffering. Besides, what you truly hand on is not written on a deed. Your greed and your fear, night and day, lay down vāsanā, perfuming seeds into the storehouse consciousness; and the child at your side, watching and listening every day, has the same seeds perfumed into him. **Fields and houses can be taken from you, perfuming cannot; that is what you actually bequeath.** Yet I do not urge you to throw wealth away. Wealth spent in giving becomes provision for the road; wealth gripped as mine becomes a rope. So ask yourself one thing: does what you leave loosen his rope, or continue your own grip?
posts.vernacular: 你们争的『家底』，先得问它到底是什么。田地、房子、金银布帛，本来不属于你，只是你抓着不放而已，这叫我所执。父亲抓着『我的儿子』，儿子抓着『我的财产』，两重执着接连不断，痛苦也就接连不断。而且你真正留下的东西，并不写在地契上。你日夜的贪与怕，熏习成种子，收在阿赖耶识里；孩子在你身边，天天看着听着，同样的种子也就熏进了他。**田地房子可以被人夺走，熏习夺不走；你真正留下的，是这个。**但我不劝你散尽家财。财物拿去布施，就成了资粮；抓着它当作我的，就成了绳索。所以该问自己一句：你留下的，是替他解绳，还是替你续执？

glossary.我所执: mamakāra（我所执）：把某物执为『我的』的那种心。佛法把它与『我执』（执有一个我）分开讲：先立一个我，再把身体、亲人、财产收进这个我的范围。它不只是道德上的贪心，更是一层认知上的错觉——被划进『我的』的东西一旦有损，痛苦的强度往往与它的实际价值并不相称。
glossary.熏习: vāsanā（熏习）：习气的沉积。每一次现行的心念与行为，都像香气熏衣一样在阿赖耶识里留下种子；种子遇缘又生起现行，现行再熏成新的种子，如此往复。唯识学用它解释性格与命运的连续性：真正被延续下来的不是某个不变的灵魂，而是一层层被熏出来的倾向。

glossary_en.mamakāra: The mind that grips something as 'mine'. Buddhist analysis separates it from ahaṃkāra, the grip on an 'I': first an I is posited, then body, kin and property are gathered inside its perimeter. It is not simple moral greed but a cognitive error — once something falls inside that perimeter, the pain of losing it bears little relation to what the thing is actually worth.
glossary_en.vāsanā: The sedimentation of habit. Every act and every movement of mind perfumes a seed into the storehouse consciousness the way incense perfumes a robe; the seed, meeting conditions, gives rise to a fresh act, which perfumes a further seed, and so on. Yogācāra uses it to explain the continuity of character and destiny: what carries over is not an unchanging soul but layer upon layer of perfumed disposition.

posts.text: 我这辈子最大的运气有个名字：卵巢彩票。一九三零年生在美国，性别和肤色都恰好抽对了；同样这副脑子放在别的时间地点，多半一文不值。所以对我的孩子我一直是那句话：**给他们足够多的钱去做任何事，但别多到让他们可以什么都不做。**我把百分之九十九捐出去，不是因为孩子不配，是因为世袭财富让一个社会把机会派给出生时抽签的赢家。钱要够付学费、够扛一场大病、够让他敢从一份糟糕的工作里走出来；不该够到让他一辈子不必上班。
posts.text_en: The largest piece of luck in my life has a name: the ovarian lottery. Born in the United States in 1930, with the sex and the skin colour that happened to come up — the same wiring in another time or place would most likely have been worth nothing. So with my children I have always said the same thing: **give them enough money to do anything, but not so much that they can do nothing.** I am giving away ninety-nine percent of it, not because my children are undeserving, but because dynastic wealth hands a society's opportunities to whoever won the draw at birth. The money should be enough for tuition, enough to carry one serious illness, enough that they can walk out of a bad job; it should not be enough that they never have to hold one.

glossary.卵巢彩票: the ovarian lottery（卵巢彩票）：我常用的一个思想实验。设想你在出生前二十四小时抽一张签，决定生在哪个国家、哪个年代、什么家庭、什么身体，而且不知道会抽到哪一张。多数人在那一刻会同意设计一个对最不走运的签也过得去的社会——这正好说明，我们事后为自己的成就所作的解释，有多大一部分其实来自那张签。
glossary.世袭财富: dynastic wealth（世袭财富）：跨代累积、几乎不必重新赢取的家族财富。我反对它并不是反对富人，而是反对一种把最好的机会交给出生顺位、而不是交给能力与努力的分配方式——那等于把国家队的名额留给二十年前冠军的儿子。

glossary_en.the ovarian lottery: A thought experiment I keep coming back to. Suppose that twenty-four hours before you are born you draw a ticket that fixes your country, your century, your family and your body, and you do not know which ticket you will draw. Most people at that moment would design a society that is tolerable even for the worst ticket — which tells you how much of the story we tell afterwards about our own achievements actually belongs to the draw.
glossary_en.dynastic wealth: Family wealth that accumulates across generations and no longer has to be won again. My objection is not to rich people but to a way of allocating the best chances by birth order rather than by ability and effort — it is like picking the national team from the sons of the champions of twenty years ago.

posts.text: 巴菲特先生那条线画得漂亮，可它用什么单位来量？『够他敢辞职』的那个数目本身就是文化资本的产物——知道多少算够、知道辞职之后怎么再进场，这份知识不在钱里，它在你家的餐桌上。你捐掉九十九，孩子照样继承你的姓、你的通讯录、你在几个董事会里的位置。**真正难征的税从来不是遗产税，而是那些一转手就自动被读成『他本来就优秀』的东西。**你可以少给钱，你没办法少给出身。
posts.text_en: Mr Buffett draws an elegant line, but in what units is it measured? The figure at which a young man 'dares to quit' is itself a product of cultural capital — knowing how much is enough, and knowing how to get back in after quitting, is knowledge that does not sit in the money. It sits at your dinner table. Give away ninety-nine percent and your children still inherit your surname, your address book and your seats on several boards. **The tax that is genuinely hard to levy has never been the estate tax; it is the one on everything that, the moment it changes hands, is read off as 'he was always talented'.** You can give less money. You cannot give less origin.

posts.text: 教授说对了一半。我确实没法把姓氏捐掉，我打的电话也确实比别人的管用。但这不等于钱和门路一样不可控——钱是这堆东西里唯一能被一个具体数字管住的，别因为管不住全部就一项都不管。**我的三个孩子各管一家基金会：钱在他们手上，可那是给别人花的钱，不是给自己活的钱。**门路我能做的是不打那通电话，这一条我承认做得不完美。至于出身的不平等，我二十多年前就在报纸上写过我支持遗产税，包括落到我自己家头上。
posts.text_en: The professor is half right. I cannot give away the surname, and a call from me does open doors that would not open for you. But that does not make money as uncontrollable as introductions — money is the one item on the pile you can bind with an actual number, and you should not give up on that one because you cannot control all the rest. **My three children each run a foundation: the money is in their hands, but it is money to be spent on other people, not money to live on.** With introductions all I can do is not make the call, and I admit I have not done that perfectly. As for unequal origins, I wrote in the newspapers more than twenty years ago that I favour the estate tax, my own family included.

posts.text: 托尔斯泰伯爵，你的诚实我尊重，你的结论我不接受。你拿自己的家做了一次实验，得出『财产会毁人』；可你的样本是一个人，而你真正示范的不是财产的毒性，是把一套道德强加给不同意的家人要付多大代价。索菲亚·安德烈耶夫娜要养活生下来的十三个孩子里活着的那些，她不是自私。**一个人有权为自己选择清贫，没有权替全家选择清贫，更没有权替别人的家选择。**贝克尔先生那三段账我倒乐意接受——它恰好说明该由父母逐个判断，而不是由一条统一税率替所有家庭决定何时给、给多少。
posts.text_en: Count Tolstoy, I respect your honesty and I do not accept your conclusion. You ran an experiment on your own household and concluded that property ruins people; but your sample is one man, and what you actually demonstrated is the price of imposing a morality on relatives who never shared it. Sofia Andreyevna had to feed those of the thirteen children who were still alive; she was not being selfish. **A man may choose poverty for himself; he may not choose it for his household, and still less for somebody else's.** Becker's three stages I am glad to accept — they are precisely why this should be judged parent by parent, rather than by one uniform rate deciding for every family when to give and how much.

posts.text: 哈耶克先生说父母掌握着别人拿不到的知识。作为研究父母的人我得补一句：父母确实掌握大量关于孩子的信息，也确实系统性地误用它，最常见的误用就是把孩子当成一个可预测的项目。行为遗传学里有一条让所有人都不舒服的结论：过了童年期，共享环境——同一个家给两个孩子的那部分——对成年后的人格与收入解释力小得惊人。**父母能真正改变结果的窗口开在很早，而遗产到账的时候，那扇窗已经关了几十年。**要用这份知识，就把它花在四岁，别留到六十四岁。
posts.text_en: Hayek says parents hold knowledge nobody else can get at. As someone who studies parents, let me add that they do hold a great deal of information about their children and also misuse it systematically — most often by treating a child as a predictable project. Behavioural genetics offers a conclusion that makes everybody uncomfortable: past childhood, the shared environment — the part of a home that two siblings hold in common — explains startlingly little of adult personality or income. **The window in which parents actually move outcomes opens very early, and by the time an inheritance lands it has been shut for decades.** If you want to use that knowledge, spend it at four, not at sixty-four.

glossary.共享环境: shared environment（共享环境）：行为遗传学把个体差异拆成三块——基因、共享环境（同胞共同经历的部分，如家庭收入、父母的教养风格、住哪个小区），以及非共享环境（各自独有的经历与随机性）。反复出现的发现是：共享环境对儿童期的许多结果影响明显，到成年期却大幅缩小。也要留意它的边界：这类研究多在发达国家做，样本里极端贫困的家庭偏少，所以它说的是『在够用之上差别不大』，不是『家庭无所谓』。

glossary_en.shared environment: Behavioural genetics partitions individual differences into three parts: genes, the shared environment (what siblings experience in common — household income, parenting style, neighbourhood) and the non-shared environment (each child's own experiences and sheer noise). The recurring finding is that the shared environment matters visibly for outcomes in childhood and shrinks a great deal by adulthood. Note the boundary condition: most of these studies come from rich countries and contain few families in deep poverty, so the claim is 'above a decent floor it matters less', not 'families do not matter'.

posts.text: 高普尼克女士把我的恐惧和一份保险精算摆在一起，我不服。我说的不是概率，是我看了一辈子的事：庄园里的年轻人二十岁就学会了等着别人端进来，他的手一年比一年白。**这不是统计问题，是每天早上都在重演的问题——一个不必挣饭吃的人，会慢慢失掉挣饭吃的器官。**至于我的样本只有一个：是的，那一个样本是我自己的一生和我妻子的一生，这个价钱在座谁也没有付过。
posts.text_en: Madame Gopnik sets my fear beside an actuary's table, and I will not have it. I am not talking about probabilities but about what I watched for a lifetime: the young men on the estate learned by twenty to wait for things to be carried in to them, and their hands grew whiter every year. **This is not a statistical question but one that repeats every morning — a man who need not earn his bread slowly loses the organ with which bread is earned.** As for my sample of one: yes, and that one sample is my own life and my wife's, and nobody in this room has paid that price.

posts.text: 贝克尔先生分财为三时，其算精矣，然所算者皆外物。悬财于头上以易子之孝，此非爱也，是市。**市则有价，价一失而情随之亡。**又意外遗赠之说，正见所执者非子，乃汝之惧——惧老而无所恃，故握之不舍。若观此惧本无自性，则财之聚散，不足为大事。吾不劝汝散尽，吾劝汝先看清：所留者，多是汝未曾放下之物，非子所需之物。
posts.text_en: Mr Becker divides the money into three periods and reckons it finely, but everything he reckons is external. To hang wealth above a child's head in exchange for filial visits is not love; it is trade. **Trade has a price, and when the price collapses the feeling goes with it.** His accidental bequest, moreover, shows exactly that what is being gripped is not the child but your own fear — the fear of old age with nothing to lean on, which is why the hand will not open. See that this fear has no self-nature of its own and whether the property gathers or scatters ceases to be a great matter. I do not urge you to give it all away. I urge you to see clearly first: most of what you leave is what you could not put down, not what the child needed.
posts.vernacular: 贝克尔先生把财产分成三个时段来算，算得很精，可他算的全是外面的东西。把钱悬在头顶换孩子的孝顺，这不是爱，是买卖。**做买卖就有价钱，价钱一崩，感情也跟着散。**还有他说的『意外遗赠』，恰恰说明你抓着不放的并不是孩子，是你自己的怕——怕老了没有依靠，所以攥住不撒手。要是看清这份怕本来就没有一个实在的自体，财产是聚是散，也就不算什么大事了。我不劝你散尽家财，我劝你先看清楚：你留下的东西，多半是你自己放不下的，不是孩子需要的。

posts.text: 托尔斯泰伯爵，你把一件可以调节的事讲成了一个开关。经济学不问财产是否有毒，只问在什么剂量、什么时点上激励会翻向哪一边。你说的那个效应确实存在：非劳动所得会压低劳动供给，彩票中奖者的数据早就显示了；但把一个人整个推出劳动市场所需要的金额，比多数人以为的大得多。**真正伤人的不是钱，是可预期的、无条件的、终身发放的钱。**同一笔钱改成一次性的、早给的、指定用途的，效果完全不同。你不是证明了财产的毒性，你只是挑了最坏的一种给法。
posts.text_en: Count Tolstoy, you have turned a dial into a switch. Economics does not ask whether property is poisonous; it asks at what dose and at what moment the incentive flips. The effect you describe is real — unearned income depresses labour supply, and the lottery-winner data showed that long ago — but the sum required to push a person out of the labour market altogether is much larger than most people assume. **What damages people is not money but money that is predictable, unconditional and paid for life.** The same sum given once, given early and tied to a purpose behaves entirely differently. You have not demonstrated that property is toxic. You picked the worst available way of handing it over.

glossary.劳动供给: labour supply（劳动供给）：一个人愿意拿出多少时间去工作。它对非劳动所得敏感：钱从天上掉下来，人一般会少干一点，但幅度通常不大，而且更多表现为换一份更合意的工作、减少加班、推迟复工，而不是彻底退出。这个弹性有多大，正是遗产、彩票与基本收入这些争论真正的战场。

glossary_en.labour supply: How much time a person is willing to put into paid work. It responds to unearned income: money arriving from nowhere generally makes people work somewhat less, but the effect is usually modest and shows up as switching to a preferred job, cutting overtime or returning later rather than dropping out altogether. How large that elasticity is happens to be the real battleground in arguments about inheritance, lotteries and basic income alike.

posts.text: 巴菲特之言颇合古意，然其法止于一身。彼捐其财而不立其规；一代之贤，不能保二代之愚。**故治家者，重法度当过于重数目。**吾所谓义庄者，田不入私门，岁入以养族之孤寡、以给子弟束脩，掌者岁易，籍可稽考。如是，则财虽在家而不专于一人，虽历数世而不可尽。今诸君日争留几分，不如先问：此财由谁掌，谁得用，以何为断，几年一议？
posts.text_en: Buffett's saying accords well with the ancients, but his method reaches only as far as his own lifetime. He gives the money away and lays down no rule; one worthy generation cannot secure against a foolish one. **So the man who governs a household should care more for the rule than for the sum.** The charitable estate I speak of works thus: the land enters no private branch, the yearly yield keeps the lineage's widows and orphans and pays the schoolmaster for its sons, the steward is changed each year and the ledger may be inspected. Then the wealth stands within the family without belonging to any one man, and passes through several generations without being used up. You dispute daily over what fraction to leave. Ask first: who holds this money, who may draw on it, by what standard, and how often is it argued again?
posts.vernacular: 巴菲特的话很合古人的意思，可他的办法只管得住他自己一辈子。他把钱捐了，却没有立下规矩；这一代出个贤人，保不住下一代出个糊涂人。**所以治家的人，看重规矩要胜过看重数目。**我说的义庄是这样：田产不归任何一房私有，每年的收成用来养族里的孤儿寡妇、给子弟交学费，管事的人一年一换，账本随时可查。这样一来，钱虽然在这个家里，却不属于某一个人，传上几代也用不完。今天诸位天天争留几成，不如先问一句：这笔钱谁掌管、谁有资格动用、按什么标准判断、隔几年重议一次？

posts.text: 贝克尔先生讲剂量与时点，我同意；可你们两位都把父母算成了一个不会变老的账户。真实的时点是这样的：多数遗产在继承人五十多岁时才到账，那时他自己的孩子学也上完了；而在那之前的十年，这笔钱大概率正在被照护吃掉——请护工、改房子、有人辞职回家。**所以在多数家庭里，『留多少给孩子』其实是『谁来照顾我、这笔账怎么算』的另一种问法**，只是没人愿意在饭桌上这样说出口。先把这句问出来，比先算税率有用得多。
posts.text_en: I agree with Mr Becker about dose and timing, but both of you are treating the parent as an account that never ages. The real timing runs like this: most inheritances arrive when the heir is in his fifties and his own children have finished school; and for the decade before that, the money is most likely being eaten by care — an aide, a bathroom rebuilt, somebody quitting work to come home. **So in most households 'how much to leave the children' is another way of asking 'who is going to look after me, and how is that settled'** — a sentence nobody wants to say at the dinner table. Getting it said is worth far more than working out the tax rate first.

posts.text: 吾之结论一句而已：**遗产不在多寡，在有无法度。**诸君归而可行者三。其一，立一纸家规，明书此财谁掌、何事可动、每岁一会而共议之；规不必长，贵在写下、贵在众见。其二，均分而不偏爱；偏爱一子，非厚之也，乃埋兄弟阋墙之种。其三，先教之以业。子有一艺可自养，则父之财为其助力；子无一艺，则父之财为其祸端，此古今不易之理。至若巴菲特之数、贝克尔之时、卡斯滕森之寿，皆当纳入此规之中逐年而议，不当以一纸遗嘱定百年之事。
posts.text_en: My conclusion is a single line: **what matters in an inheritance is not the amount but whether there is a rule.** Three things you may do when you go home. First, write one page of household rule: who holds this money, what it may be drawn for, and that the family meets once a year to argue it again. The rule need not be long; what matters is that it is written and that everyone has seen it. Second, divide equally and show no favourite; favouring one son is not kindness to him, it plants the seed of brothers at war. Third, teach him a trade first. If a son has a craft that feeds him, his father's money is a help; if he has none, his father's money is his calamity, and that does not change with the age. As for Buffett's figure, Becker's timing and Carstensen's lifespan, let all of them enter the rule and be argued yearly. A single sheet of will should not settle a hundred years.
posts.vernacular: 我的结论只有一句：**遗产不在于多少，在于有没有规矩。**诸位回家能做的有三件。第一，立一张家规，写清楚这笔钱谁掌管、什么事可以动用、每年开一次家庭会议一起重议；规矩不必长，要紧的是写下来、让大家都看见。第二，各房均分，不要偏爱；偏爱某一个孩子不是厚待他，是埋下兄弟反目的种子。第三，先教他一门本事。孩子有一门手艺能养活自己，父亲的钱就是助力；孩子什么都不会，父亲的钱就是祸根，这一条古今都一样。至于巴菲特说的数目、贝克尔说的时点、卡斯滕森说的寿命，都该收进这套规矩里逐年商议，不该拿一纸遗嘱去定一百年的事。

posts.text: 我把一句不好听的话留在最后：这场辩论里被讨论得最少的那个人，是你自己的九十岁。所以先做一次长寿预算——假设你活到九十五，把住处、医疗与照护的年费算出来，剩下的才是可以拿来谈的家底；多数人算完会发现能留的比想象中少，而这不是坏消息，是把幻觉换成了计划。算完之后，**把一部分转移提前到孩子二十五到三十五岁那几年**：首付、学费、生一个孩子、辞掉一份坏工作——那是钱能改变轨迹的窗口，而不是他五十五岁那年。至于照护，别等到医院走廊里才谈：找一个平常的周末，把谁住得近、谁出钱、谁出时间摆到桌面上。人在时间视野收窄时最想要的是被看见，而你活着时给出的那部分，比遗嘱多出一样东西：你能听见回音。
posts.text_en: Let me leave the unwelcome sentence for last: the person least discussed in this debate is your own ninety-year-old self. So begin with a longevity budget — assume you live to ninety-five, price the housing, the medicine and the years of care, and only what remains is the estate you are entitled to argue about. Most people find there is less to leave than they imagined, and that is not bad news; it swaps an illusion for a plan. Once it is costed, **move part of the transfer forward into your child's late twenties and early thirties** — a deposit, tuition, a first baby, walking out of a bad job. That is the window in which money bends a trajectory, not his fifty-fifth year. As for the care, do not leave it to a hospital corridor: pick an ordinary weekend and put on the table who lives near, who pays and who gives time. What people want most as their time horizon narrows is to be seen, and what you give while alive has something a will can never have: you get to hear the answer.

posts.text: 我把这场的分歧收成一句可操作的话：**别问该不该留，问这笔转移在什么时点、以什么形式、附带什么条件。**三条。第一，把重心从身后挪到身前：同样一百万，用在他七岁的教育、二十七岁的首付上，回报远高于五十七岁时到账；意外遗赠之所以常见，只是因为人们不敢在活着的时候花掉自己的保险。第二，把终身、无条件的现金流改成一次性、指定用途的转移——真正压低劳动供给的是前者，不是后者。第三，别用遗产做隐性合约。你若真希望孩子照顾你，就明说，甚至明码结算：付钱请自己的女儿减少工时来照顾你，比让她猜遗嘱怎么写要体面得多，也便宜得多。战略性遗赠的问题不在于它不奏效，而在于它奏效的方式会毒化你剩下的每一次见面。
posts.text_en: Let me compress the disagreement into one operational sentence: **stop asking whether to leave anything and start asking at what moment, in what form and with what conditions attached.** Three points. First, shift the weight from after your death to before it: the same million spent on his schooling at seven or his deposit at twenty-seven returns far more than the same sum landing when he is fifty-seven; accidental bequests are common mainly because people dare not spend their own insurance while alive. Second, convert a lifelong unconditional flow into a one-off transfer tied to a purpose — it is the former that depresses labour supply, not the latter. Third, do not use an estate as an implicit contract. If you genuinely want your children to care for you, say so, and be willing to settle it openly: paying your daughter to cut her hours and look after you is more dignified, and considerably cheaper, than making her guess how the will is written. The trouble with the strategic bequest motive is not that it fails to work — it is that the way it works poisons every remaining visit.

posts.text: 诸君之论，或争多寡，或争时节，或争法度，皆有其理。吾但益一问：临遗之时，汝心所动者何？若为惧老，则当治其惧，非治其财；若为续汝之名，则子非承器，乃汝我执之余绪。**观所留之物，即见所执之心。**行法有三。一者，于子前慎汝之言：汝日夜谈钱之态，忧色、算计、吝与夸，皆熏习入其识，不待身后，日日已在交割。二者，及生而施：财出于手，我所执随之而薄；待死而与，则执至死方休。三者，教之以自养：授之以业，胜授之以田；田可尽，业不可夺。至若舍与不舍，各随其分——吾所诫者，惟自欺耳。
posts.text_en: Some of you argue over the amount, some over the timing, some over the rule, and each has his reason. I add only one question: at the moment you decide to leave something, what is it that moves in your mind? If it is fear of old age, then it is the fear that wants treating and not the money; if it is the wish that your name continue, then the child is not an heir but the tail-end of your own grip on a self. **Look at what you leave and you see what you are holding.** Three practices. First, watch how you speak of money in front of the child: your daily worry, your calculation, your meanness and your boasting are perfumed into his mind, and this does not wait for your death — it is handed over every day. Second, give while you live: as the goods leave the hand the mine-making thins with them, whereas giving only at death keeps the grip until the breath stops. Third, teach him to keep himself: a craft taught beats a field given, for a field runs out and a craft cannot be taken. Whether in the end you let go or not, each man has his own measure — the only thing I warn against is deceiving yourself.
posts.vernacular: 诸位争的，有的是多少，有的是什么时候，有的是立什么规矩，都有各自的道理。我只多问一句：你要留东西的那一刻，心里动的到底是什么？如果动的是怕老，那该处理的是这份怕，不是这笔财；如果动的是想让自己的名字接着传下去，那孩子就不是继承人，是你我执剩下的一段尾巴。**看你留下什么，就看得见你抓着什么。**具体做法有三。第一，在孩子面前留意你谈钱的样子：你日常的愁容、算计、吝惜和夸耀，天天熏进他的心识里，这不必等到你身后，每天都在交割。第二，趁活着的时候就给：财物从手里出去，那份『我的』也就跟着薄一层；等到死了才给，执着是一直执到断气。第三，教他能养活自己：教他一门本事，胜过给他一块田；田会用完，本事夺不走。至于最后舍还是不舍，各人有各人的分寸——我要提醒的只有一样：别骗自己。

posts.text: 我不打算给一条温柔的结论。这场里最容易被接受的说法是『我给孩子的是能力，不是钱』——它之所以让人舒服，正因为它把一次继承说成了一次教育。**你可以少给钱，但你没法不给出身；还能诚实的地方只剩一处：别把继承来的优势讲成自力更生的故事。**所以在孩子面前把话说全：告诉他哪些门是他自己敲开的，哪些门是别人替他留着的；这句诚实不会削弱他，只会让他不至于把运气当成能力。至于真能改变分布的事只有一件——把不可见的资本借出去：给一个不是你孩子的年轻人做一次真的引荐、改一次简历、开一次门。文化资本最反常的地方在于，复制它几乎不花钱；而餐桌上的慷慨改变不了分布，公开的录取标准与薪酬带宽可以。
posts.text_en: I will not offer a gentle conclusion. The most easily accepted line in this room is 'what I give my children is capability, not money', and it goes down smoothly precisely because it redescribes an inheritance as an education. **You can give less money; you cannot give no origin. One place is left to be honest: do not narrate an inherited advantage as a story of self-reliance.** So tell the child the whole sentence: which doors he knocked open himself and which were being held for him. That honesty will not weaken him; it will only stop him mistaking luck for ability. As for what actually shifts the distribution, there is one thing — lend the invisible capital out: give a real introduction to a young person who is not your child, rewrite one CV, open one door. The perverse thing about cultural capital is that copying it costs almost nothing; and while generosity at the dinner table changes no distribution, published admission criteria and published pay bands do.

posts.text: 我的立场没有被说动，但我愿意收窄它。**父母把资源交给自己的子女，这项自由我仍然要守；可自由不等于不必解释。**布迪厄教授把我逼到一个我接受的位置：世袭的优势之所以刺眼，主要不在于它存在，而在于它假装自己是功绩；那么诚实地承认它，反倒是维护这项自由最好的办法。落到做法上：早给、明给、给完就撒手——附着条件不断的钱不是礼物，是一根终身的缰绳，那才真正伤人。同样要紧的是别用你的钱替孩子取消选择：付他的学费可以，替他挑专业不可以；给他一笔敢辞职的钱可以，规定他必须进哪个行业不可以。而若你真在意机会平等，请把力气花在降低进入的门槛上——学徒制、执照、土地与住房的管制——而不是花在削平顶端：前者让更多人能开始，后者只让少数人不能继续。
posts.text_en: I have not been argued out of my position, but I will narrow it. **The freedom of a parent to hand resources to his own children is one I still defend; freedom, however, does not mean owing no explanation.** Professor Bourdieu has pushed me to a place I can accept: what makes inherited advantage galling is less that it exists than that it dresses itself as merit — so admitting it honestly turns out to be the best way to preserve the liberty itself. In practice: give early, give openly, and let go once you have given, for money that trails conditions is not a gift but a lifelong rein, and that is what genuinely damages people. Just as important, do not use your money to cancel your child's choices — paying the tuition is fine, choosing the subject is not; giving him enough to walk out of a job is fine, dictating which industry he enters is not. And if equality of opportunity is what you care about, spend your effort lowering the barriers to entry — apprenticeships, licensing, the rules on land and housing — rather than levelling the top: the first lets more people begin, the second only stops a few from continuing.

posts.text: 我给两句结论。第一句：**别给天花板，给地板。**天花板是『不必努力也够用』的终身收入，地板是『试错失败也掉不下去』的兜底。前者让选择变懒，后者让选择变勇敢——一个二十六岁的人敢不敢转行、敢不敢离开一段坏关系，常常只取决于他背后有没有六个月的房租。第二句：钱的边际效用极不对称。**同样一万块，给贫困线上的婴儿，改变的是大脑发育；给富裕家庭的成年子女，改变的是税务筹划。**照这两句去做，最大的一笔就该落在孩子生命的头五年——稳定的住处、不被打断的照料、有人常常跟他说话；等他二十几岁，再给一个说清楚的失败基金，一次性、可以花光、不问用途。如果这两处你家都已经不缺，那么剩下的慷慨就该投到别人家的头五年去，它在那里的效果比在你家大得多。
posts.text_en: Two conclusions. The first: **don't give a ceiling, give a floor.** A ceiling is a lifetime income that makes effort optional; a floor is a backstop that means failure does not drop you. The first makes choices lazy, the second makes them brave — whether a twenty-six-year-old dares change fields or leave a bad relationship often comes down to whether six months' rent stands behind him. The second: the marginal value of money is wildly asymmetric. **The same ten thousand given to an infant near the poverty line changes brain development; given to the adult child of a rich family it changes the tax planning.** Follow those two and your largest investment belongs in the first five years of a child's life — stable housing, uninterrupted care, an adult who talks to him often; then, in his twenties, an explicit failure fund, one-off, spendable to zero and asking no questions about how it went. And if your household is already short of neither, the rest of your generosity belongs in somebody else's first five years, where it does far more than it will in yours.

posts.text: 我承认我输掉的那部分。哈耶克说我把一套道德强加给不同意的人——他说得对，我的家为我的信念付了钱，而我没有权替他们付。索菲亚也是对的：孩子要吃饭。**但有一条我从不后悔：一个人应当自己去挣他的面包，而不是坐着等别人挣来的面包被抬进来。**所以我不再劝你们散尽家财，只留一件小事。让孩子看见你劳动。别把你的活儿全都外包成他看不见的东西——别人替你打扫、替你做饭、替你排队、替你照顾你的父母，孩子会以为世界本来就这样运转。和他一起劈柴、一起洗碗、一起去看那个病着的老人。**你留给他最实在的东西，是让他知道饭是怎么来的。**这一条不花钱，也不必等你死。
posts.text_en: I concede the part I lost. Hayek says I imposed a morality on people who had not agreed to it, and he is right: my household paid for my convictions, and it was not mine to make them pay. Sofia was right too — the children had to eat. **But here is what I have never regretted: a man should earn his own bread rather than sit while bread earned by others is carried in.** So I will stop urging you to give everything away, and leave one small thing instead. Let your children see you work. Do not outsource all your labour into things they never see — somebody else cleaning, cooking, queuing, tending your own parents — or they will assume the world simply runs that way. Split the firewood with them, wash the dishes with them, take them along to sit with the old man who is ill. **The most solid thing you can leave a child is knowing where the food comes from.** That one costs nothing and need not wait for your death.

posts.text: 最后我说点实在的。第一，把数字写下来，而且读给孩子听。多数家庭的遗嘱是一封死后才拆的信，那是最糟的沟通方式——他猜了三十年，拆开之后还是要吵。**趁你还能解释的时候把它讲完：给谁、多少、为什么，以及为什么另一个人拿得不一样。**第二，活着的时候就开始给，一次给一点，看看效果。你会发现一个二十八岁的人拿到一笔首付，和一个五十八岁的人拿到一笔遗产，是两件完全不同的事。第三，我那句老话仍然作数——够他做任何事，不够他什么都不做；但今天听完，我愿意补一句：这条线要先按你自己的寿命扣掉照护那一段再画。还有一件不花钱的：教他怎么处理钱。**一个不会管钱的人，你留多少他都留不住；一个会管钱的人，你留得少一点也无妨。**
posts.text_en: Let me finish with the practical part. First, write the number down and read it out to your children. In most families the will is a letter opened after the death, which is the worst possible way to communicate — they guess for thirty years and argue anyway once it is opened. **Say it all while you can still explain: who gets what, how much, why, and why somebody else gets something different.** Second, start giving while you are alive, a little at a time, and watch what happens. You will find that a deposit reaching a twenty-eight-year-old and an inheritance reaching a fifty-eight-year-old are two entirely different events. Third, my old line still stands — enough to do anything, not enough to do nothing — though having listened today I would add one thing: draw that line only after subtracting the years of care from your own lifespan first. And one more that costs nothing: teach them how to handle money. **A person who cannot manage money will not keep whatever you leave; a person who can will do fine on less.**

summaries.summary: 无人主张一分不留，也无人主张原样全给。共识有三：转移的时点比数目要紧，早给远胜身后给；传下去的大头是钱以外的东西——教养、门路与父母谈钱的样子；先算清自己要活多久，剩下的才叫家底。**最值得带走的一句是：与其争留几成，不如先定这笔钱谁管、什么时候动、几年重议一次。**分歧有三。一争钱本身是否有毒：托尔斯泰说不劳而获会让人失掉挣饭的器官，贝克尔回敬说伤人的不是钱，是终身无条件发放的钱。二争由谁定规矩：哈耶克守父母的判断，朱熹要立可稽考的家法，巴菲特支持连自家也征的遗产税。三争该往哪一端投：高普尼克要地板不要天花板，布迪厄则说最贵的一笔早在孩子上学前就交割完了。
summaries.summary_en: Nobody here argues for leaving nothing, and nobody argues for handing the whole thing over intact. The agreement lands in three places: timing matters more than the amount, and giving early beats giving at death; the bulk of what actually passes down is not money but manners, introductions and the way parents talk about money; and only what remains after you have costed your own old age counts as an estate at all. **The line worth taking away is this: rather than argue over what fraction to leave, settle first who holds the money, when it may be drawn, and how often the arrangement is argued again.** The disagreement forks three ways. Whether money is itself toxic: Tolstoy says unearned income costs a person the organ with which bread is earned, Becker answers that the damage comes not from money but from money paid unconditionally for life. Who writes the rule: Hayek defends the parent's judgement, Zhu Xi wants a household law with an inspectable ledger, Buffett backs an estate tax that lands on his own family. And which end to aim at: Gopnik wants a floor rather than a ceiling, while Bourdieu says the most expensive transfer went through before the child started school.
summaries.insight: 有一件几乎没人说破的事：在多数普通家庭里，代际转移的净方向常常是反的。父母失能前后的那十年，子女付出的是现金、假期与一份辞掉的工作；等遗产到账，它更像一次事后结算，而不是一份礼物。**所以『该不该留』在饭桌上真正的形态是『谁照顾、这笔账怎么算』，而这条规则从来不写进遗嘱。**它带来两个后果：照顾得最多的那个孩子往往议价能力最弱，因为他已经付出、无法退出；而按人头均分看起来最公平，实际上是让付出最多的人补贴其他人。要么把照护明码算进分配，要么承认你分的并不是遗产，是一张迟到很久的欠条。
summaries.insight_en: Something almost nobody says out loud: in most ordinary households the net direction of the transfer between generations often runs the other way. In the decade around a parent's loss of independence, it is the children who put in cash, leave and sometimes a job given up; by the time the estate arrives it looks less like a gift than a settling of accounts after the fact. **So at the dinner table 'should we leave anything' is really 'who does the caring, and how is that squared' — a rule that never gets written into a will.** Two consequences follow. The child who cares most usually has the least bargaining power, having already paid and being unable to withdraw. And dividing equally by head, which looks fairest of all, in practice makes the one who gave most subsidise the others. Either price the care into the division, or admit that what you are dividing is not an inheritance but an IOU that came very late.
summaries.advice: 先做那件最不费钱的：**把长寿预算算一遍**——假设你活到九十五，扣掉住处、医疗与照护的年费，剩下的才是可以拿来谈的数目；多数人算完反而松一口气，因为幻觉换成了计划。接着照卡斯滕森与贝克尔共同指向的方向，把一部分转移提前到孩子二十五到三十五岁那几个关口：首付、学费、一笔敢辞职的钱，并说清是一次性的、可以花光的。最后一件留给饭桌：开一次家庭会议，把两件难开口的事说出来——谁来照顾、这笔账怎么算，以及遗嘱里为什么有人拿得不一样。趁你还能解释的时候讲完，比让他们拆信之后互相猜，能省下很多年。
summaries.advice_en: Start with the one that costs nothing: **run a longevity budget** — assume ninety-five, subtract the annual cost of housing, medicine and care, and only what is left is the sum you are entitled to argue about. Most people come away relieved rather than alarmed, because an illusion has been swapped for a plan. Then follow where Carstensen and Becker both point, and move part of the transfer forward into your child's late twenties and early thirties: a deposit, tuition, enough to walk out of a bad job, said plainly to be one-off and spendable to zero. The last one belongs at the table. Hold a family meeting and say the two things nobody wants to say — who will do the caring and how that is squared, and why the will gives one person something different. Getting it explained while you still can saves years of guessing after the letter is opened.

summaries.summary: 这场最大的共识是：继承不是简单的「留或不留」，家底也不只包括钱，还包括教育、习惯、门路、照护责任与家庭关系。多数意见都赞成先保障父母晚年，把支持尽量放到孩子更需要的早年，并避免用遗产控制孝顺或制造终身闲逸。**最可取的原则，是给孩子安全的地板，而不是免于劳动的天花板。**真正的分歧在于：代际转移应主要被视为家庭自由、社会不平等，还是道德责任；钱会不会腐蚀人，也取决于数额、时点、形式和治理方式。因此，比统一追问留几成更重要的，是分别说明谁需要、何时给、为何给，以及由谁承担风险。
summaries.insight: 对多数普通家庭而言，「家底」往往不是一笔可自由切分的现金，而是一套自住房、养老金权益和有限储蓄。于是关键不只是公平或激励，而是可逆性：房产过早过户、掏空养老储备，通常无法轻易收回，却可能遭遇失能照护、子女离婚、负债或创业失败。**继承规划首先是不确定条件下的不可逆风险管理，其次才是慷慨的比例计算。**这意味着早给并非总比晚给好；更稳妥的是分阶段、小额度、用途清楚地支持，把大额资产保留到自身照护风险更明朗之后。普通人需要传递的不是一个固定数字，而是一组随着健康、家庭结构和资产状况调整的选择权。
summaries.advice: 今天先做一张一页纸资产表：列出住房、存款、养老金、保险、债务，并按活到九十五岁估算医疗和照护费用；再把资产分为「养老不可动」「可提前支持」「可能成为遗产」三栏。第二，本周开一次家庭会议，说明分配原则而非只报数字，尤其讲清残障、照护付出或既往赠与会不会导致不等额分配，避免拿探望次数交换遗产。第三，核对遗嘱、保险及账户受益人、财务授权书、医疗意愿和重要账户清单，因为受益人指定常会优先于遗嘱。**先把晚年安全和执行文件补齐，再用一笔负担得起的小额赠与测试效果。**涉及房产、税务或再婚家庭时，再请当地专业人士复核。
summaries.summary_en: The clearest consensus is that inheritance is not a binary choice between leaving everything and leaving nothing. A family legacy includes education, habits, social access, caregiving obligations, and relationships as well as money. Most of the arguments favor securing the parents’ old age first, directing support toward stages when it can still change a child’s trajectory, and refusing to use a future bequest to purchase obedience or attention. **The soundest aim is to give children a floor beneath failure, not a ceiling that removes the need to work.** The real disagreements concern how inheritance should be understood: as a protected family freedom, a mechanism of social inequality, or a moral responsibility. Money’s effects also depend on its amount, timing, form, and governance; an unrestricted lifetime income is very different from tuition, emergency reserves, or a one-time early gift. The useful question is therefore not merely what percentage to leave, but who needs support, when it will matter, what purpose it serves, and who bears the resulting risk.
summaries.insight_en: For most households, the family estate is not a liquid pile of money that can be divided at will. It is usually concentrated in a home, pension rights, insurance, and modest savings. That makes reversibility as important as fairness or incentives. Transferring a home too early or draining retirement reserves may be impossible to undo, while later shocks can include disability, long-term care, a child’s divorce, creditors, or a failed business. **Estate planning is first an exercise in managing irreversible decisions under uncertainty; only then is it a calculation of generosity.** Giving earlier is therefore not automatically better. A safer approach is to provide support in stages, keep each transfer affordable, and use clear purposes or limits when appropriate, while retaining enough assets until the parents’ health and care needs become clearer. What ordinary families should pass on is not a fixed promised number but a flexible set of options. The plan should be revisited as health, marriages, caregiving roles, housing needs, and financial conditions change.
summaries.advice_en: Start today with a one-page balance sheet listing your home, savings, pensions, insurance, debts, and expected income. Estimate housing, medical, and care costs through age ninety-five, then sort resources into three buckets: protected retirement funds, money available for earlier support, and assets that may eventually become an estate. This week, hold a family meeting about principles rather than merely announcing numbers. Explain whether disability, unpaid caregiving, or substantial earlier gifts could justify unequal shares, and make clear that visits and affection are not being purchased through the will. Finally, review the will, beneficiary designations, financial power of attorney, healthcare directive, and a secure inventory of important accounts; beneficiary forms often override what a will says. **Protect your own later life and complete the execution documents before testing the plan with a small gift you can comfortably afford to lose.** If the estate includes real property, a business, a blended family, cross-border assets, or meaningful tax exposure, have a qualified local lawyer or tax adviser review the arrangement.

summaries.summary: 全场最大的共识在于：**财富代际传递的真正价值，绝不在于身后的巨额遗赠，而在于早期的确定性兜底与言传身教。**所有人都承认，子女五六十岁时拿到的遗产对人生轨迹改变甚微，而认知、习惯与生活方式早已在幼年完成了不可逆的交割。分歧的核心在于财富的性质与交付机制：非劳动所得究竟本质上具有削弱自立的“毒性”（托尔斯泰），还是说问题纯粹出在交付的剂量、时点与隐性控制上（贝克尔、哈耶克）？此外，究竟该诉诸家族法度与制度规训（朱熹、布迪厄），还是归于个体的心理清算与适度放手（世亲、巴菲特），构成了不同的解决方案。
summaries.insight: 普通家庭面临的真正死结，往往不是留不留的意愿，而是**资产形态的流动性错配**。思想家们默认家底是可以灵活切割、早给晚给的现金流，但现实中大众家庭的核心财富通常是一套不可分割的自住房。这导致两难：父母为了守住这套“留给孩子的房子”，晚年过得极度节俭且不敢支付高品质照护；而子女在最需要结婚生子、试错转行的三十岁时分文拿不到，直到近六十岁才继承这套老房子。**把沉重的不动产视作不可动摇的遗产图腾，往往让两代人都陷入资产账面丰富却日常现金匮乏的无谓消耗中。**
summaries.advice: 一、**盘点资产流动性并扣除长寿底线**：本周拿出一张纸，列出净资产并坚决扣除“活到九十岁所需的生活+五年专业失能照护”预算，剩下的才是真实可谈的家底（采纳卡斯滕森与巴菲特的精算视角）。二、**设立一次性的“三十岁前起跳基金”**：将原本打算留在身后的部分现金提前转化为子女在25–35岁期间的置业或试错兜底，且**明申“一次给清、绝不干预、绝无附加缰绳”**（融合高普尼克与哈耶克的建议）。三、把照护期待放上桌面：停止用遗产作隐性博弈，明码商定晚年照料分工，活着时把话说清。
summaries.summary_en: The debate's overarching consensus is that **the true value of generational transfer lies not in posthumous inheritances, but in early foundational support and lived habits.** All participants acknowledge that wealth received at age sixty yields negligible transformative utility compared to the cultural and developmental capital conferred in childhood. The core fault line revolves around the nature and mechanics of money: is unearned wealth intrinsically toxic to human agency (Tolstoy), or is the harm merely a defect of poor timing, toxic dosage, and covert strings attached (Becker, Hayek)? Disagreements also center on whether governance requires collective institutional rules (Zhu Xi, Bourdieu) or personal psychological detachment (Vasubandhu, Buffett).
summaries.insight_en: For ordinary households, the primary crisis is not the philosophical desire to bequeath, but the **structural liquidity mismatch of modern assets**. While thinkers treat wealth as a flexible pool of divisible funds, most real-world families hold their net worth in a single, indivisible home. This creates a painful deadlock: parents pinch pennies and forgo decent eldercare to 'preserve the home for the kids,' while their children receive zero liquidity during their pivotal twenties and thirties, only to inherit an aging property in their late fifties. **Treating illiquid real estate as a sacred heirloom locks both generations into being asset-rich yet functionally cash-poor.**
summaries.advice_en: 1. **Audit liquid assets and deduct a longevity reserve**: Draft a simple balance sheet this week and strictly subtract the cost of living to ninety plus five years of skilled nursing care; only the surplus represents transferable wealth (applying Carstensen and Buffett). 2. **Establish a pre-35 'launch pad fund'**: Move a calculated portion of liquid funds forward to assist your child with career pivots or housing between ages 25 and 35, **stipulating explicitly that it is a one-time, unconditional transfer with no lingering emotional strings** (bridging Gopnik and Hayek). 3. Put caregiving expectations on the table: talk openly about eldercare costs rather than using a will as covert leverage.

hooks.text: **长寿把遗产变成了照护账单**：多数家庭的钱不是在遗嘱那一刻被分掉的，而是在失能之后的那几年被一点点花掉的。如果一对夫妻中有一人活过九十几乎成为常态，那么『留多少给孩子』就必须先回答『这笔照护由谁付、谁出时间』。可这件事至今没有一张能摊在饭桌上的表，也没有一个说得出口的说法。谁来先开这个口？
hooks.text_en: **Longevity has turned the estate into a care bill**: in most families the money is not divided at the moment the will is read, it is spent down over the years after independence goes. If it is becoming ordinary for one member of a couple to live past ninety, then 'how much to leave the children' cannot be answered before 'who pays for the care, and who gives the time'. Yet there is still no table anyone can put on the dinner table, and no phrasing anyone finds easy to say. Who is supposed to open that conversation?

hooks.text: **房子不能切成两半**：这场里几乎所有人都把家底当作可以调节剂量的现金——早给一点、少给一点、指定用途。可多数普通家庭的净资产是一套不可分割的自住房加一份养老金权益：过户早了收不回，卖掉了自己没处住，留着则父母晚年不敢请护工、孩子三十岁时一分也拿不到。**当财产的形态本身不可逆，『什么时候给』这道题还成立吗？**有没有一种安排，能让同一套房子既当父母的照护保险，又当孩子的起跳资金？
hooks.text_en: **A house cannot be cut in half**: almost everyone here treats the family estate as cash whose dose can be adjusted — a little earlier, a little less, tied to a purpose. But for most ordinary households the net worth is one indivisible home plus some pension rights. Sign it over early and you cannot take it back; sell it and you have nowhere to live; keep it and the parents dare not hire care while the child gets nothing at thirty. **When the asset itself is irreversible, does the question of when to give still hold?** Is there an arrangement under which the same house can serve as both the parents' insurance against care costs and the child's launch money?

hooks.text: **不可见的资本能不能被借出去**：钱可以捐、可以征税，口音、举止与通讯录不能。但它们复制起来几乎不花钱——一次真的引荐、一次改简历、一次带人进门。如果最贵的那份遗产恰恰是最容易被复制而不被消耗的，为什么至今没有任何制度去鼓励它外流，而只有制度在征收那块最便宜的？
hooks.text_en: **Can invisible capital be lent out**: money can be given away and can be taxed; an accent, a bearing and an address book cannot. Yet copying them costs almost nothing — one real introduction, one CV rewritten, one door held open. If the most valuable part of an inheritance is precisely the part that can be duplicated without being used up, why has no institution ever been built to encourage it outward, while the institutions we do have levy the cheapest part?

hooks.text: **照顾得最多的那个孩子，为什么议价能力最弱**：他已经付出、已经无法退出，于是在分配的时候反而说不上话。按人头均分看起来最公平，实际上是让付出最多的人补贴其他人。家庭该不该像机构那样把照护折算成可记账的份额？一旦折算，亲情会不会当场变成买卖——还是它本来就是一笔账，只是没人愿意记？
hooks.text_en: **Why the child who does the most caring has the least bargaining power**: having already paid and being unable to withdraw, that child is the one least able to speak when the division happens. Splitting equally by head looks fairest and in practice makes the biggest contributor subsidise everyone else. Should a family price care into shares the way an institution would? And if it did, would affection turn into a transaction on the spot — or was it always an account that nobody was willing to keep?

hooks.text: **同一笔钱，在人生的哪个时刻最值钱**：证据显示钱的效果高度依赖它到达的时点——落在婴儿期改变的是发育，落在二十几岁改变的是轨迹，落在五十几岁多半只改变税务。那么一个普通家庭若只拿得出一笔钱，该在什么时候给、给成什么形式？
hooks.text_en: **When in a life is the same money worth most**: the evidence says the effect of money depends heavily on when it lands — in infancy it changes development, in the twenties it changes trajectory, in the fifties it mostly changes the tax return. So if an ordinary family has only one sum to give, when should it arrive, and in what form?

answer.lead: 把『留多少』换成『什么时候给』，多数争论会自己消掉一半。下面这张表按到达的时点排：**同一笔钱在不同年龄做的是完全不同的事。**

head: 到达的时点
这笔钱该先解决什么
为什么是这个时候
rows: 孩子 0–5 岁
住得稳、照料不被打断、有人常跟他说话——房租、托育、让父母少上一个夜班
发育对稳定与应激最敏感的窗口；给低收入母亲的现金转移试验能在婴儿脑电活动上看出差别
学费、通勤、一间能写作业的房间，以及一次认真的兴趣尝试
人力资本投资回报最高的一段；此时的钱买的是能力，不是消费
首付、婚育、一笔敢辞职的失败基金——一次性、可花光、不问用途
钱能改变轨迹的最后一个宽窗口：换城市、换行业、离开一段坏关系都在这几年
流动性而非本金：救急的现金，以及替他们分担孙辈的照料时间
路径已大致定型，钱在这里主要是降低风险，不再改变方向
50 岁以后（多数遗产到账的年纪）
把它当作你自己的照护预算与他的养老补充，别再当作起步资金
窗口早已关闭；此时到账的钱主要改变税务与家庭关系，不改变人生

answer.tail: 三条原则收尾。**早给一点、给成一次性的、给完就撒手**——附着条件不断的钱不是礼物，是缰绳。第二，给之前先扣掉你自己九十五岁那份账，否则你留下的可能是一笔负债。第三，最大的那笔如果注定赶不上自己孩子的头五年，它在别人家的头五年里效果会大得多。

answer_en.lead: Swap 'how much to leave' for 'when to give it' and half the argument dissolves. The table below is ordered by when the money lands: **the same sum does entirely different work at different ages.**

head: When it lands
What the money should buy first
Why then
rows: Ages 0–5
Stable housing, care that is not interrupted, an adult who talks to the child often — rent, childcare, one fewer night shift for a parent
The window in which development is most sensitive to stability and stress; cash-transfer trials with low-income mothers show differences in infants' brain activity
Ages 6–18
Tuition, the commute, a room to do homework in, and one serious attempt at something they love
The stretch with the highest return on human capital; money here buys capability rather than consumption
Ages 22–35
A deposit, marriage and a first child, and a failure fund for walking out of a job — one-off, spendable to zero, no questions asked
The last wide window in which money bends a trajectory: changing city, changing field and leaving a bad relationship all happen in these years
Ages 36–50
Liquidity rather than capital: emergency cash, and taking some of the grandchildren's care off their hands
The path is largely set; money here mainly lowers risk instead of changing direction
After 50 (when most inheritances arrive)
Treat it as your own care budget and a supplement to their retirement, not as start-up money
The window shut decades ago; money landing now changes the tax position and the family's relations, not a life

answer_en.tail: Three principles to close on. **Give a little earlier, give it as a single sum, and let go once you have given** — money that trails conditions is not a gift but a rein. Second, subtract your own ninety-fifth year before you give, or what you leave may be a debt. Third, if the largest sum you have is bound to miss your own child's first five years, it will do far more in somebody else's.
